Between the time of al-Ash‘ari and al-Ghazali, some thinkers fiercely opposed philosophy without this kind of intellectual understanding or clarity. Quite the opposite: they showed a striking ignorance of philosophy. One revealing example appears in Jamal al-Din Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn al-Abbas al-Khwarizmi (d. 382 AH/993), The Useful in the Sciences and the Destruction of Worries, al-Matba‘a al-Sharqiyya, 1328 AH, pp. 61–62. He wrote: “They—that is, the philosophers—are a people from among the Greeks who became so confused in their doctrines that they fell into the valley of bewilderment and derangement, which resembles madness without being madness. They were perplexed in divine matters and based their views on pure whim and unsupported claims. They claim to be the cleverest of God’s creation, yet the course of their doctrine shows that they are the most ignorant of God’s creation and the most foolish of people. The foundation of atheism and heresy rests on their doctrine, and all unbelief is a branch of theirs (...) They used to experiment with preventing reproduction, and their leader Plato the atheist—may God curse him—said to Moses son of Amram, God’s messenger and interlocutor: ‘I will believe everything you say except your statement: the Cause of Causes spoke to me.’ Look at the belief of this wicked man: he called God’s messenger a liar and believed that God Most High has no speech at all (...) He also believed that the world is eternal. His companions, such as Aristotle, Socrates, Hippocrates, and Galen, are all certainly the atheists of their age and the heretics of their time (...) They are polytheists and atheists—may God curse them!”↩︎

As for al-Hamdani, whom Qadi Sa‘id mentions here, al-Qifti refers to him in Accounts of the Sages and says that he died in prison in Sana‘a in 334 AH/946. Al-Hamdani wrote Secrets of Wisdom and Genealogies of Himyar. He also wrote philosophical studies on the origin of the world and on the principles of logic and kalam. Among the earlier writers, Ibn Khaldun is an exception here. He does not believe that Arabs are by nature incapable of receiving philosophy, because he does not classify peoples’ intellectual abilities on a racial basis. Instead, he traces them to natural and social factors—to civilization and social development. He uses the same factors to explain why most philosophers in our heritage were non-Arabs. See the Muqaddima, book 6, chapter 13, Beirut ed., pp. 860–866.↩︎

Here too, Ibn Khaldun is an exception. Speaking about the translation of Greek philosophy into Arabic, he writes: “Muslim thinkers devoted themselves to it and mastered its branches. Their investigations reached the furthest limits in these sciences. They agreed with many views of the First Teacher [Aristotle] and disagreed with many others, accepting or rejecting them because his fame had become the standard of reference. They wrote major works on these subjects and surpassed those who had come before them in these sciences. Among the greatest of them within the Muslim community were Abu Nasr al-Farabi and Abu Ali Ibn Sina in the East, and Qadi Abu al-Walid Ibn Rushd and the minister Abu Bakr Ibn al-Sa’igh in al-Andalus, along with others who reached the highest level in these sciences.” Muqaddima, book 6, chapter 13, p. 865, Beirut ed. This does not contradict Ibn Khaldun’s statement in chapter 15 of the same book, p. 971, that Muslim philosophers adopted the doctrines of earlier thinkers, led by Aristotle, following his view “step for step except in a few matters.” In that later passage, Ibn Khaldun is speaking specifically about the structure of the cosmos, not philosophy as a whole. He is discussing the philosophers’ denial concerning the world of the celestial spheres.↩︎

A story is told about Ibn al-Salah that is said to explain his hostility to logic. According to the story, he secretly traveled to Mosul to study logic with the hadith scholar Kamal al-Din ibn Yunus al-Mawsili, a contemporary of Ibn Khallikan (1211–1283). Ibn al-Salah, however, was unable to understand logic. His teacher advised him to give up studying it, and he did so, publicly declaring hostility toward Ibn Yunus under the pretext of defending religion. Tash Kubra Zada was more a historian of philosophy than a philosopher. He wrote The Key to Happiness and Lamp of the Abode of Sovereignty, printed in Hyderabad: vol. 1 in 1328 AH and vol. 2 in 1329 AH. The work gives a critical account of the development of Muslim knowledge of the sciences. In it, he describes the “philosophical sciences” as “the true sciences that do not change with changing times, governments, or religions.” He places logic among the “divine sciences” and links philosophy with Sufism when he says that the philosophical sciences may be gained through rational investigation or through purification—meaning purification of the soul through spiritual discipline and struggle, that is, Sufism. In the terminology of early historians, classification into “classes” (tabaqat) was not based on social class in the modern sense. It usually meant chronological grouping. A “class” could therefore mean a generation of poets, hadith scholars, philosophers, and so on, with a generation usually spanning between ten and twenty years. Sometimes a geographical criterion was used, as Ibn Sa‘d did in his Great Book of Classes when he arranged biographies of the Companions according to the cities where they settled. See Ibn Sa‘d, Classes, Dar Sadir/Dar Beirut, 1957, Ihsan Abbas’s introduction, vol. 1, p. 12. Books of tabaqat, then, are specialized biographical works devoted to a particular group of historically important people. This form of writing among Arabs and Muslims goes back to the third century AH. Al-Waqidi may have been the first to write in this form, followed by his student Muhammad ibn Sa‘d; both wrote about hadith scholars. In the same century, many literary writers produced books on classes of poets, such as Ibn Sallam’s Classes, Ibn Qutayba’s Poetry and Poets, and Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s Classes of Poets. Later came works on the “classes” of physicians, sages, Shi‘is, Shafi‘is, and so on.↩︎

The history of Arabic literature gives us an example in which most of these personal, class, and ideological motives come together, along with a desire to flatter the ruling power. Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz (247–296 AH), whose caliphate lasted no more than a day and part of another day, wrote a book called Classes of Poets, containing biographies of about 127 male and female poets from the Abbasid period. Three points about this book were noted by its editors, Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj and Abbas Iqbal. First, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz ignores several of the greatest poets of his age, including Ibn al-Rumi (221–283 AH). He also ignores Ibn al-Rumi in his book al-Badi‘. Why, when Ibn al-Rumi was such an important poetic figure in the Arabic tradition? The editor and publisher Abd al-Sattar Farraj links this omission to two positions taken by Ibn al-Rumi. First, Ibn al-Rumi had satirized al-Mu‘tazz, the author’s father, after he was removed from the caliphate. Second, Ibn al-Rumi “was closely associated with al-Qasim ibn Ubayd Allah, one of Abdallah ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s enemies, who advised that he be arrested when al-Mu‘tadid died.” Here the motive is personal. Second, Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s book gives biographies of poets who praised or had connections with the Abbasid caliphs (...) and gathers poetry stamped with the outlook of poets dependent on Abbasid caliphs, ministers, and leading officials. It also tries to reveal the relationship between each poet and the person he praised (Abbas Iqbal). Here the motive is class-based and ideological. Third, the editors observe that despite Ibn al-Mu‘tazz’s fame and the importance of his book, later biographers rarely mentioned it; “it was as though most of them did not know it.” Abd al-Sattar Farraj points to a convincing political reason: “al-Muqtadir returned to the caliphate and remained caliph for more than twenty years after Ibn al-Mu‘tazz was killed. There is no doubt that most transmitters do not favor someone from whom power has turned away and whom the events of time have brought down.” This is a case of flattering the ruling power. See Ibn al-Mu‘tazz, Classes of Poets, edited by Abd al-Sattar Ahmad Farraj, Dar al-Ma‘arif, Egypt, no date, pp. 10, 12, 583, 588.↩︎
